sentences: Your 24-hour window starts when your previous daily or weekly rest ends.
Within that 24 hours you must have taken a new daily rest.
If the part of that rest falling inside the 24 hours is at least 9 hours but less than 11, it counts as a reduced daily rest.
The Commission's Guidance Note 7 dates from 2015, before the 2020 Mobility Package, but it agrees with the current Regulation on this point.
It adds three practical rules:
- If your rest lasts longer than the legal minimum, the next 24-hour period starts at the actual end of that rest.
- If the 24 hours run out while you are still resting, and the minimum was not reached inside that window, the next 24 hours start when you end a rest of at least 9/11 hours and go back to work.
- If you never take a valid daily rest, enforcers split your activity into back-to-back 24-hour blocks, counted from the end of your last valid rest.
With two or more drivers on board (multi-manning), the window is 30 hours instead of 24.

- it carries materials, equipment or machinery you use in your own work, such as your carpentry tools;
- you stay within a 100 km radius of your company's base (80 km is fine);
- driving is not your main activity;

On an occasional passenger service, the 45-minute break due after 4.5 hours of driving can be replaced by two breaks of at least 15 minutes each.

All drivers may also use the general split: at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30 minutes.

The third paragraph of Article 7 allows the 45-minute break due after 4.5 hours of driving to be replaced by two breaks of at least 15 minutes each for occasional passenger services.
Article 7 says the two breaks are distributed over the driving period referred to in the first paragraph, which is the 4.5-hour period.
The second paragraph of Article 7 allows any driver to replace the break with at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30 minutes.
Article 5(1) of Directive 2002/15/EC says mobile workers shall in no circumstances work more than six consecutive hours without a break.
